summary: Defines how the DNS stores mapping information that e-mail gateways need to map RFC 822 domain names to X.400 O/R names and back. It is an experimental protocol. It was replaced by RFC 2163.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet phone book can also hold the translation guide between two mail address styles. A newer version replaced it.

questions: how to convert x.400 to email
subtitle: Using DNS to store email address translation between two mail systems

tldr.problem: Email gateways need to translate between X.400 and RFC 822 (Internet) email addresses, but storing mapping tables centrally requires constant updates and distribution to all gateways.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1664 proposes using the Domain Name System (DNS) to distribute and query mapping rules via a new PX resource record, creating an X.400 name space under X42D.country codes in the DNS tree.
tldr.outcome: This approach enables dynamic, distributed management of address mappings and was experimentally deployed. The specification was later refined and replaced by RFC 2163.

facts.value: Reserved label X42D under each country code

facts.value: Hyphen -h-, dot -d-, space -b-, other chars as -DDD-

today: RFC 1664 is Experimental and was replaced by RFC 2163. The PX record and DNS-based address mapping approach were validated through test deployments but remained experimental as wider adoption of the DNS infrastructure took time.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
RFC 1327 specifies how to convert email addresses between X.400 (an international standard system) and RFC 822 (Internet email) format. As described in RFC 1327 Appendix F, this requires a mapping database. The traditional approach keeps static tables at each gateway, but this has significant operational problems: tables must be coherent across all gateways, updates must be distributed to all sites, and the process is slow.

RFC 1664 proposes a better approach: storing mapping rules in the Internet Domain Name System (DNS) instead. The DNS is a proven distributed system with facilities for authority delegation, dynamic updates, and efficient queries. This solves the distribution problem and allows the mappings to be managed decentrally according to national and regional boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: Gateways need a translation guide between two types of email. Instead of everyone having a paper copy that must be mailed out and updated, the idea is to put the rules in the Internet phone book where everyone can look them up anytime.

sections.title: DNS Mapping Rules and Resources
sections.content:
RFC 1664 defines how RFC 1327's three mapping tables are represented in DNS. Table 1 translates X.400 to RFC 822 addresses, while Table 2 and the Gate table translate RFC 822 to X.400. The new PX resource record (type number 26) stores mapping rules with fields for PREFERENCE (priority, like MX records), MAP822 (the RFC 822 part), and MAPX400 (the X.400 part in domain name syntax).

Each RFC 1327 mapping rule is encoded as a DNS PX record. For Table 1 entries, the DNS name is an X.400 domain in domain-name syntax with a X42D.country suffix. For Table 2 and Gate entries, the name is an RFC 822 domain. Both RFC 1327 'table2' and 'gate' entries use the same syntax; a trailing ".G." suffix on MAPX400 distinguishes gate entries from table 2 entries.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say: for translations from one system to another, store them in a special DNS record (PX) with a priority number. Use special names for X.400 addresses so they fit in the DNS.

sections.title: X.400 Name Space Structure
sections.content:
Instead of creating a global X.400 registry (like in-addr.arpa), RFC 1664 nests X.400 address spaces under national boundaries. Each country gets a branch under a reserved label X42D placed under its two-letter ISO country code. This respects X.400's country-oriented structure and aligns with the Internet's regional delegation model.

Under each country's X42D node, the X.400 hierarchy is represented: ADMD (Administration Management Domain), PRMD (Private Management Domain), O (Organization), and OU (Organizational Unit). Special encoding rules translate X.400 attributes (which use characters invalid in DNS labels) into legal DNS label syntax: hyphens become "-h-", dots become "-d-", spaces become "-b-", and non-alphanumeric characters become 3-digit decimal ASCII codes enclosed in hyphens.
sections.plainLanguage: Create a folder in DNS under X42D.uk (or X42D.fr, etc.) for that country's X.400 addresses. Translate X.400's special characters into DNS-friendly codes so they fit in the folder structure.

sections.title: Encoding and Query Examples
sections.content:
A Table 1 RFC 1327 rule like PRMD$ab.ADMD$ac.C$fr#ab.fr# becomes a wildcard PX record *.PRMD-ab.ADMD-ac.X42D.fr. IN PX 50 ab.fr. PRMD-ab.ADMD-ac.C-fr.. A Table 2 rule ab.fr#PRMD$ab.ADMD$ac.C$fr# becomes *.ab.fr. IN PX 50 ab.fr. PRMD-ab.ADMD-ac.C-fr..

When a gateway translates an RFC 822 domain, it queries DNS for the appropriate PX record. When translating from X.400, it converts the X.400 address to domain-name syntax, applies the Country Code convention (omitting the C-cc suffix as redundant), and queries the resulting DNS name. The DNS wildcard mechanism returns the longest matching rule in a single query, eliminating the iteration required with static table lookups.
sections.plainLanguage: To find how to translate an address, turn it into a DNS name and look it up. The DNS will give you back the translation rule automatically.

sections.title: Administration and Migration
sections.content:
RFC 1664 envisions three models for gateway management: table-based (traditional static tables), DNS-based (this proposal), and X.500-based (using a different directory system). Table-based domains can submit their mapping information to an International Mapping Table coordinator, which then distributes it via DNS for sites that lack their own nameservers. Migration can follow the pattern used for the transition from static hosts.txt files to DNS.

The specification also discusses potential coordination with X.500 directory systems, including the possibility of dynamic alignment mechanisms that transparently make DNS mappings available in X.500 and vice versa, creating a unified transparent directory service.
sections.plainLanguage: Some places will use old-style tables, some will use DNS, and some will use a different system. They can all work together: central coordinators can publish table-based mappings in DNS for everyone else to share.
